extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of art history; critics and practitioners interested in evaluating Renaissance painting and sculpture
extracted.subtask_description: Critical evaluation criteria for fifteenth-century (Renaissance) painting and sculpture, focusing on qualities like imaginative vision, use of colour, compositional treatment, relief technique, finish, and the balance between universality and individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of poetic narrative and formal painting qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'poetical painter' blends the charm of story and sentiment (the medium of poetry) with the charm of line and colour (the medium of abstract painting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how successfully an artist unites narrative/poetic content with formal qualities of drawing and colour. Examples: Botticelli's Dante illustrations where poetic meaning is carried by line and colour; avoid mere literal illustration—the visual work should convey the poem's mood and meaning, lowering the key when translating poetic language into image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visionary imagination vs naturalistic transcription
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist 'usurps the data before [him] as the exponent of ideas, moods, visions of its own'—rejecting, isolating, and recombining observed facts to produce an original mood or vision rather than a mere transcription of outward appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work transforms observed reality to express a singular mood or insight (visionary) rather than simply copying nature (naturalist). Positive sign: inventive alterations that deepen the work's emotional or intellectual effect; negative sign: purely documentary depiction lacking personal vision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative composition and temporal condensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compositions may be 'crowded with incident, blending three phases of the same scene into one plate'; narrative space can contain multiple temporal phases or incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the handling of sequential or multiple moments within a single image: are they combined coherently to enhance meaning, or do they create pictorial confusion? Example: Botticelli's crowded Dante illustrations—successful when they express a painter's vision rather than slavish literalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness and original visual invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A true painter's vision produces original pictorial inventions (e.g., the fire taking hold on upturned soles; imaginative rendering of Centaurs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for striking visual inventions that go beyond literal description and reveal the artist's imaginative response to the subject. Such inventions mark the work as creative rather than merely illustrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of grotesque and poetical grotesques
rubrics_metrics.description: Grotesques in poetic source-material can be a stumbling-block; a painter should lower the key of grotesque images when translating them into visual form, choosing subjects and tone appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether grotesque elements are adapted sensitively (e.g., choosing calmer phases like Purgatorio for illustration) or awkwardly reproduced, which can break pictorial propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathy and portrayal of complex humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist's 'morality is all sympathy'—an interest in men and women in their mixed, uncertain condition, conveying the true complexion of humanity rather than idealised goodness or absolute evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the artist represents human complexity—nuanced, sympathetic portrayals that acknowledge doubt, wistfulness, or inner conflict are valued over simplified moralising types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent development of a distinct type (portrait-figure types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Working out and repeating a distinct, peculiar type (e.g., Botticelli's Madonnas) that gains expressive power through recurrence: 'he has worked out in them a distinct and peculiar type, definite enough in his own mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether repeated types deepen meaning and create a coherent artistic persona (positive) or become mechanical and monotonous (negative). Note identifying features (from text: wan colour, abstract facial lines, white light from below, child's distant gaze).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour as expressive/imaginative agent, not mere naturalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour should function as 'a spirit upon [things] by which they become expressive to the spirit'—imaginative colouring (minor tones, colder lights) that serves mood and idea rather than copied natural colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate colour for expressive intent: use of subdued or 'minor' tones to convey mood (as in Botticelli), restraint rather than warm naturalistic brilliance. Beware cloying or purely decorative sunshine that undermines subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of classical (pagan) imagery with Christian sentiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical story is 'imaginative material' to be received and assimilated; artists may reconcile pagan imagery with Christian subjects, producing a mixed mythology of new tone and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge success by the coherence of assimilation—classical motifs should be meaningfully integrated (e.g., Venus or fauns in the presence of the Madonna) rather than superficially pasted on. Consider whether the mixture yields new imaginative effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope of art: avoiding overt moral ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Art does its most sincere and surest work when 'undisturbed by any moral ambition'; Botticelli 'sets for himself the limits within which art... does its most sincere work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work overreaches into didactic moralizing at the expense of pictorial sincerity. Valued works maintain aesthetic aims and human sympathy without forced moral preaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of low relief to etherealize sculpture and avoid hard realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Low relief is the means by which Tuscan fifteenth-century sculptors 'meet and overcome' sculpture's tendency to hard realism, obtaining a pathetic suggestion of wasting and etherealisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating sculpture, consider relief depth as an expressive choice: low relief can subdue solid form, reduce harsh shadows, and enhance delicacy and expressive subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtle shadowing and refinement over strong chiaroscuro
rubrics_metrics.description: These sculptors are 'haters of all heaviness and emphasis, of strongly-opposed light and shade,' seeking 'last refinements of shadow' almost invisible except in strong light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the handling of light and shadow for delicacy and nuance rather than dramatic chiaroscuro; success is measured by subtle gradations that suggest rather than assert form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of expression (capturing transient life and feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole essence of their work is EXPRESSION—the passing of a smile, the ripple of the air—sculpture concerned with the play of life rather than mere solid form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether sculpture captures fleeting affects and lived presence; attention to small, transient details (smile, ripple, gesture) is a positive sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allgemeinheit (Greek universality/type) vs expressive individuality trade-off
rubrics_metrics.description: The Greek way seeks 'breadth, generality, universality' (Allgemeinheit) by extracting the type in the individual, purging accidental detail—this secures universality but can sacrifice individual expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing works influenced by classical ideals, weigh the value of universal type versus loss of individual expression; consider whether the abstraction serves the work's aims or diminishes human specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of studied incompleteness to suggest life (Michelangelo's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Michelangelo leaves 'nearly all his sculpture in a puzzling sort of incompleteness' which acts as an 'equivalent for colour'—a way of etherealising form, suggesting breath and pulsation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider unfinished or partially finished surfaces as deliberate expressive devices that can create tension and a sense of emergence; judge whether incompleteness enriches rather than appearing careless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing universality and individuality (Luca della Robbia approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A midway system combining Greek Allgemeinheit and Michelangelo's studied incompleteness: intense, individualised expression united to a conventional subduing of form and lower relief to avoid hard realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how successfully a sculptor balances type and individual character, using conventionalisation and relief choices to secure both repose and expressive specificity (example: sepulchral portraits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching medium, material, and site to intended aesthetic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Material and locality matter: Luca's pale blue-and-white earthenware evoke 'the milky sky' and 'lose their savour when moved from their birthplace'; medium shapes the work's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess an artwork in relation to its material properties and original setting; judge whether the chosen medium enhances the intended visual and emotional effects and whether relocation diminishes them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sculptural means to mere applied colour in sculpture
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'use of colour in sculpture is but an unskilful contrivance'—nobler sculpture seeks the equivalent of colour by its own means rather than borrowing from painting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging polychromy or painted sculpture, consider whether coloration is an integral, skilful enhancement or a crude substitute for sculptural technique; prefer solutions that achieve colour-equivalents through form, finish, and surface treatment.
